title: Nmap Pro
description: Advanced scan types, evasion, NSE, and outputs.

1.title: Scan types
1.body:
## The complete scan menu

| Flag | Name | How it works | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-sS` | SYN | SYN → RST (without connecting) | fast, the standard |
| `-sT` | Connect | full handshake | when you don't have root |
| `-sN` | NULL | packet with no flags | evading basic firewalls |
| `-sF` | FIN | FIN flag only | same |
| `-sX` | XMAS | FIN+PSH+URG (lit up like a tree) | same |
| `-sU` | UDP | UDP packets | DNS/SNMP/DHCP |
| `-sA` | ACK | ACK flag only | mapping firewall rules |

## FIN/NULL/XMAS: the "weird" scans that work

Old firewalls only filter SYN packets (the ones that try to CONNECT). A
FIN or NULL packet sent to an OPEN port on a Unix host gets no response (the stack
silently ignores it). A CLOSED port answers with RST.

```text
FIN → open port       →  silence      ← open!
FIN → closed port     →  RST          ← closed
FIN → firewall        →  nothing      ← filtered (ambiguous with open)
```

Their weak point: modern firewalls and Windows answer RST to EVERYTHING (a deviation
from the RFC), which makes it impossible to tell the states apart. But against a Linux host
without a stateful firewall: it works.

## ACK scan (-sA): the firewall map

It doesn't detect open ports — it detects WHICH PORTS the firewall FILTERS (unfiltered vs
filtered). You use it AFTER a SYN scan to understand the rules.

```bash
nmap -sA -p 80,443,8080 10.10.10.5   # what does the FW filter?
```

2.title: Evasion
2.body:
## The three layers of evasion

### 1. Timing templates (-T)

```bash
nmap -T0 10.10.10.5    # paranoid: 5 min between packets. Undetectable by rate-based IDS
nmap -T2 10.10.10.5    # polite: slow but reasonable
nmap -T4 10.10.10.5    # aggressive: fast (the default in labs)
nmap -T5 10.10.10.5    # insane: VERY fast, loses results, SOS in the SIEM
```

### 2. Fragmentation and decoys

```bash
nmap -f 10.10.10.5           # fragments probes into 8-byte packets
nmap -ff 10.10.10.5          # even smaller fragments
nmap -D RND:10 10.10.10.5    # 10 random decoy IPs + yours
nmap -S <spoof_ip> 10.10.10.5  # full spoofing (only works with a zombie scan)
nmap --source-port 53 10.10.10.5   # source port 53 (DNS): many FWs allow it
```

### 3. Decoys in practice

`-D` makes the target see the scan coming from 11 IPs (10 fake ones + yours). The
admin has to investigate 11 sources. In an AUTHORIZED pentest, decoys are
agreed in advance (the SOC must be able to tell legitimate traffic apart from the test).

## In real pentest life

Evasion is NEVER total: a SIEM with correlation detects patterns even if you fragment.
Evasion slows down and complicates detection, and in white/grey-box engagements it is
coordinated with the SOC (time window, known source IPs).

In CTFs and labs: `-T4` and off you go. In a client's production environment: coordinate, use `-T2`,
and limit the port scope.

3.title: NSE and outputs
3.body:
## NSE: 600+ ready-made scripts

```bash
# Useful categories
nmap --script vuln 10.10.10.5            # looks for known vulnerabilities
nmap --script auth 10.10.10.5            # tries anonymous/default logins
nmap --script discovery 10.10.10.5       # enumerates information
nmap --script smb-vuln* 10.10.10.5       # all the SMB ones

# Specific ones you will ALWAYS use in Windows pentests
nmap --script smb-vuln-ms17-010.nse -p 445 10.10.10.5   # EternalBlue
nmap --script smb-enum-shares.nse -p 445 10.10.10.5     # SMB shares

# Web
nmap --script http-enum.nse -p 80 10.10.10.5            # common paths
nmap --script http-title.nse -p 80 10.10.10.5           # page titles
nmap --script ssl-heartbleed.nse -p 443 10.10.10.5      # Heartbleed
```

## Outputs: the evidence for the report

```bash
nmap -sV -oA escaneo_inicial 10.10.10.5
# generates: escaneo_inicial.nmap (human), .gnmap (grep), .xml (parseable)
```

- **`-oN`** (normal): the readable output — paste it straight into the report.
- **`-oG`** (grepable): one line per port — processable with `grep`, `awk`.
- **`-oX`** (XML): for tools like `searchsploit --nmap`.
- **`-oA`**: all three at once.

```bash
# Real pipeline: nmap → grep → searchsploit
nmap -sV -oG - 10.10.10.5 | grep open | grep -oP '\S+/\w+ open \S+ \S+' 
searchsploit --nmap escaneo_inicial.xml    # suggests exploits by version
```

## Your Nmap cheat sheet (copy it)

```bash
nmap -sn CIDR                    # discovery
nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 5000 IP  # fast full range
nmap -sV -sC -p PUERTOS IP       # versions + default scripts
nmap -sU --top-ports 20 IP       # basic UDP
nmap --script vuln -p PUERTOS IP # vulnerabilities
```

With Nmap mastered, you can move on to the web module: Burp Suite does for HTTP what Nmap
does for TCP.
